title: TypeScript Types Quick Revision: Annotations to Strict Mode
summary: Night-before revision notes on TypeScript's type system basics: annotations and inference, primitives, arrays and tuples, the any/unknown/never trio, void, enums versus union literals, and strict mode.

chapters.title: Annotations and Inference Mental Model
points: Annotation = explicit type after a colon: `let n: number = 5`; it is erased at compile time and has no runtime effect
Inference: TS derives the type from the initializer, so `let n = 5` is `number` and `const n = 5` is the literal type `5`
Annotate function parameters (never inferred from the body) and exported return types; let locals and callbacks infer
Contextual typing: `[1,2].map(x => x * 2)` infers x as number from the array type, with no annotation needed
Mistake: `let x;` with no initializer is implicitly any (evolving any); annotate it or initialize it

chapters.title: Primitives, Arrays and Tuples
points: Primitives are lowercase: string, number, boolean, bigint, symbol, null, undefined; never use the wrapper types `String`/`Number`
Arrays: `number[]` equals `Array<number>`; `readonly number[]` blocks push and index assignment
Tuple = fixed length and per-position types: `let p: [string, number] = ['a', 1]`; supports optional `[string, number?]` and labels `[name: string, age: number]`
Array vs tuple inference: `const a = ['x', 1]` infers `(string | number)[]`; add `as const` to get `readonly ['x', 1]`
Mistake: `push` on a non-readonly tuple is allowed and breaks its length guarantee; use `readonly` tuples

chapters.title: any, unknown and never
points: `any` disables checking: any operation compiles and the error surfaces at runtime, and it spreads through assignments
`unknown` is the safe top type: anything is assignable to it, but you must narrow it (typeof, instanceof, a type guard) before using it
`never` is the empty bottom type: it is the return type of functions that always throw or loop, and the type left after exhaustive narrowing
Exhaustiveness check: assign the leftover value in a switch `default` to `const _x: never = v` so a new union member becomes a compile error
Rule: use `unknown` for untrusted input such as JSON.parse results or catch variables, and avoid `any`; `any` assigns to everything while `unknown` assigns only to unknown and any

chapters.title: void and Enums vs Union Literals
points: `void` return type means the return value is ignored; a callback typed `() => void` may still return a value, but a function declared `: void` cannot return one

`void` vs `undefined`: `void` means the result is ignored, `undefined` means the result is the value undefined (since TS 5.1 neither needs an explicit `return`), and `never` means the function never returns at all
Numeric enums are reverse-mapped (`E[0]` gives the name) and accept any number in older TS; string enums are not reverse-mapped and are safer
Enums emit runtime JS objects; `const enum` is inlined and emits nothing, but it is a problem with isolatedModules
Union literals `type Dir = 'up' | 'down'` emit no JS, are structural and are tree-shakeable; prefer them, or use `as const` objects when you need runtime values (`keyof typeof Obj`)

chapters.title: Strict Mode and Common Mistakes
points: `"strict": true` in tsconfig turns on the whole family: noImplicitAny, strictNullChecks, strictFunctionTypes, strictBindCallApply, strictPropertyInitialization, noImplicitThis, alwaysStrict, useUnknownInCatchVariables, strictBuiltinIteratorReturn (TS 5.6+)
strictNullChecks: null and undefined are not assignable to other types, so `string | null` forces a check before use
noImplicitAny: a parameter with no annotation or inference is an error instead of silently any
strictPropertyInitialization: class fields must be assigned in the constructor or declared with `!` (definite assignment) or `?`

Mistakes: overusing `as` casts and the non-null `!` operator to silence the compiler, since both are unchecked and only assert; `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` is not part of strict and must be enabled separately

chapters.title: TypeScript Types Cheat Sheet
points: Annotate: `let x: T`, `function f(a: A): R`; let inference handle locals and use `as const` for literals
Collections: `T[]`, `readonly T[]`, `[A, B]`, `[a: A, b?: B]`
Escape hatches ranked: `unknown` (safe), `any` (unsafe), `as` (assertion), `!` (non-null assertion)
Special types: `void` ignored return, `never` unreachable or exhausted, `unknown` must narrow first
Choose union literals over enums; use `strict: true` and add `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` for safer indexing
